title: Height of a valuation is unchanged by algebraic extension
statement: Let $E/K$ be an algebraic extension of fields [def-pc-field-extension] [def-weil-algebraic-element]. Let $V\subseteq E$ be a valuation ring of $E$, meaning a subring such that for every $a\in E^\times$, either $a$ or $a^{-1}$ belongs to $V$. Put $A=V\cap K$. Then $A$ is a valuation ring of $K$ and contraction of prime ideals gives an order isomorphism from the prime ideals of $V$ onto the prime ideals of $A$, ordered by inclusion. In particular $V$ and $A$ have the same height, where height is the supremum of the lengths of finite strictly increasing chains of prime ideals; either both heights are finite or both are infinite.

source.place: §2.1, p. 7: correspondence of prime ideals with convex subgroups of the value group, and the finite-extension fundamental inequality $\sum_i e_{L_i/k}f_{L_i/k}\le[L:k]$ at the foot of p. 7, shortly before Lemma 2.1.2 (p. 8); algebraic height invariance is the consequence for the union of finite subextensions.

proof.text: For $x\in K^\times$, the defining alternative $x\in V$ or $x^{-1}\in V$ lies in $K$ as well, so $A=V\cap K$ satisfies the same valuation-ring condition. Also, in either $A$ or $V$, two nonzero elements are comparable for divisibility: apply that condition to their quotient. In a finite nonempty list of nonzero elements there is consequently an element dividing all the others (select successively a divisor from each pair).

source.place: Tag 052L, lemma-valuation-ring-cap-field; Tag 090Q, lemma-characterize-valuation-ring, finite-generator divisibility argument. The radical-ideal and prime-spectrum argument below is agent-written.

proof.text: Write $I_V$ for the ideal of $V$ generated by an ideal $I\subseteq A$; its elements are finite sums $\sum_i a_i v_i$ with $a_i\in I$, $v_i\in V$. We have $I_V\cap A=I$. Indeed, for a nonzero such sum $b\in A$, select a nonzero $a_j$ dividing all $a_i$ in $A$ by Step 1. Then $b/a_j=\sum_i(a_i/a_j)v_i\in V\cap K=A$, hence $b\in I$. The zero sum is already in $I$, and the reverse inclusion is immediate.

source.place: Tag 052L, lemma-valuation-ring-cap-field; Tag 090Q, lemma-characterize-valuation-ring, finite-generator divisibility argument. The radical-ideal and prime-spectrum argument below is agent-written.

proof.text: For an ideal $J\subseteq V$ put $\sqrt J=\{x\in V:\exists n\geq1,\ x^n\in J\}$. This is an ideal: it contains $0$, is closed under multiplication by $V$ and negation by taking the same exponent, and if $x^n,y^m\in J$, every term of the binomial expansion of $(x+y)^{n+m}$ is divisible by either $x^n$ or $y^m$, so $(x+y)^{n+m}\in J$. For a prime ideal $\mathfrak q\subset A$ put $P(\mathfrak q)=\sqrt{\mathfrak q_V}$. Then $P(\mathfrak q)\cap A=\mathfrak q$: if $a^n\in\mathfrak q_V$ with $a\in A$, Step 2 gives $a^n\in\mathfrak q$, and primeness gives $a\in\mathfrak q$. Conversely $\mathfrak q\subset P(\mathfrak q)$. Thus $1\notin P(\mathfrak q)$.

source.place: Tag 052L, lemma-valuation-ring-cap-field; Tag 090Q, lemma-characterize-valuation-ring, finite-generator divisibility argument. The radical-ideal and prime-spectrum argument below is agent-written.

proof.text: The ideal $P(\mathfrak q)$ is prime. If $xy\in P(\mathfrak q)$, choose $n\geq1$ with $(xy)^n\in\mathfrak q_V$. If either factor is zero it belongs to $P(\mathfrak q)$. Otherwise either $y=xc$ or $x=yc$ for $c\in V$ by Step 1. In the first case $y^{2n}=(xy)^n c^n\in\mathfrak q_V$, so $y\in P(\mathfrak q)$; in the second case $x^{2n}=(xy)^n c^n\in\mathfrak q_V$, so $x\in P(\mathfrak q)$. Together with Step 3 this proves surjectivity of contraction on prime ideals.

source.place: Tag 052L, lemma-valuation-ring-cap-field; Tag 090Q, lemma-characterize-valuation-ring, finite-generator divisibility argument. The radical-ideal and prime-spectrum argument below is agent-written.

proof.text: Fix a prime $\mathfrak p\subset V$ and put $\mathfrak q=\mathfrak p\cap A$. For $0\ne x\in V$, apply [lem-trf-valuation-value-group-torsion] to obtain $x^n=au$ with $n\geq1$, $a\in K^\times$, and $u,u^{-1}\in V$. Then $a=x^nu^{-1}\in V\cap K=A$. Since a unit belongs to no proper ideal and a prime ideal contains $x^n$ exactly when it contains $x$, we get $x\in\mathfrak p\Longleftrightarrow a\in\mathfrak q$. If $x\in\mathfrak p$, this same equality puts $x^n\in\mathfrak q_V$, so $x\in P(\mathfrak q)$. Conversely, $\mathfrak q_V\subseteq\mathfrak p$ and primeness imply $P(\mathfrak q)\subseteq\mathfrak p$. Zero belongs to both. Therefore $P(\mathfrak p\cap A)=\mathfrak p$.

source.place: Stacks Tag 0ASJ, lemma-etale-extension-valuation-ring, first proof paragraph: finite extension of fraction fields gives finite index of value groups and hence f=w h^n with n>0, f in the base valuation ring, and w a unit upstairs. The node isolates that general algebraic input, applied elementwise to K(x)/K; it does not use the étale conclusion of the lemma.

proof.text: Steps 3--5 show that contraction and $P$ are inverse bijections on prime ideals. Contraction preserves inclusions. Its inverse also preserves inclusions: $\mathfrak q\subseteq\mathfrak r$ implies $\mathfrak q_V\subseteq\mathfrak r_V$ directly from finite-sum generators, and hence $\sqrt{\mathfrak q_V}\subseteq\sqrt{\mathfrak r_V}$ by the power-membership definition. They thus form an order isomorphism. Apply the two inverse maps to any finite strict chain: strictness and length are preserved by injectivity and order reflection. The sets of possible finite chain lengths agree, so their suprema agree, including unbounded height.
